title: Image-region retrieval: cite the object, not merely the image
summary: Retrieve a bounded visual region and preserve its asset version, crop coordinates and supporting labels.
body:
Retrieve a bounded visual region and preserve its asset version, crop coordinates and supporting labels.

Index regions with their parent asset

Image-region retrieval searches a part of an image that can support a specific claim. A maintenance photo may show several pumps, warning tags and gauges; an image-level match for 'P-47 gauge' says little about which gauge carries the reading. Store asset ID, version, image dimensions, region coordinates and any reviewed label. A crop is not an independent source: it inherits access rules and revision from the parent image. Asset identity prevents a crop coordinate from silently pointing at a replacement photograph.

Generate and score candidates

Regions can come from reviewed annotations, object proposals or a grid of crops. Search their labels and visual representations, then cap the candidate window before expensive inspection. Overlapping proposals for one object should not consume every slot. Group them by parent asset and approximate overlap, retaining a precise box when evidence supports it. A predicted label is a search hint, not proof that the pictured valve is P-47. Duplicate control helps keep copied crops from masquerading as independent sightings.

Ground the claim spatially

The answer should point to a region whose visible pixels support it. A caption outside the crop may identify the object, but the caption and image need separate provenance. If the query asks whether a red lockout tag is attached, a close crop of the tag alone might hide whether it is attached to the requested pump. Keep enough surrounding context to verify the relationship without turning the citation into the whole image. Claim support must inspect the crop and its parent context.

Account for transformations

Resizing, rotation and cropping change coordinates. Store boxes in a stable source coordinate system and record any display transform; never reuse pixel positions on a newly cropped image without mapping them. Check privacy masks at the source and crop levels. A face blurred in the full image can reappear if an unredacted original is cropped and served separately. Reject regions whose bounds fall outside the asset or whose version mismatches the current display. Lifecycle rules include withdrawing all derived crops after an asset is removed.

Evaluate region-level evidence

Judge both parent-image recall and region overlap with the answer-bearing object. Include small objects, similar gauges, partially occluded labels, repeated components and misleading captions. A system that finds the correct photo but draws a box around the wrong gauge should fail. Track unsupported confident labels and missing-evidence abstentions separately. Measure the cost of finer crops against their improvement in supported claims, rather than indexing thousands of near-identical patches without a clear gain.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ImageRegion:
    asset_id: str
    version: str
    width: int
    height: int
    box: tuple[int, int, int, int]
    label: str

def checked_region(region: ImageRegion, expected_version: str) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    if region.version != expected_version:
        raise ValueError("asset version mismatch")
    left, top, right, bottom = region.box
    if region.width <= 0 or region.height <= 0 or not (0 <= left < right <= region.width):
        raise ValueError("invalid horizontal bounds")
    if not 0 <= top < bottom <= region.height:
        raise ValueError("invalid vertical bounds")
    return (left / region.width, top / region.height,
            right / region.width, bottom / region.height)

gauge = ImageRegion("plant-photo-47", "v3", 1200, 800,
                    (240, 160, 600, 560), "P-47 pressure gauge")
assert checked_region(gauge, "v3") == (.2, .2, .5, .7)
try:
    checked_region(gauge, "v2")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("stale crop accepted")

Performance and operating cost

Validating one region is O(1) time and space. A full image with R proposed regions needs storage and embedding work proportional to R, plus overlap grouping if many proposals duplicate the same object. Candidate generation can be bounded by asset and region counts; visual inspection is the costly stage. Keep source-resolution crops only for regions that survive retrieval and access checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Citing an image when the requested object is not identifiable within it.
  • Using crop coordinates from a different image version.
  • Treating a detector's label as verified identity.
  • Serving an unredacted crop of a redacted parent asset.

Validation drill

Judge 41 questions over 23 photographs containing repeated gauges, tags and valves. Score asset recall, region overlap and claim support; require rejection of stale-version boxes.

title: Event-window retrieval: answer from complete time slices
summary: Retrieve logs and measurements with explicit event time, observation time, window bounds and missing-data behavior.
body:
Retrieve logs and measurements with explicit event time, observation time, window bounds and missing-data behavior.

Define the clock and window

Event-window retrieval finds records that occurred in a requested interval, not merely records indexed recently. A query about pump P-47 alarms between 09:00 and 09:30 must use event time; observation time describes when the collector received a record. Late arrivals and device clock drift can make those differ. Store both clocks, source ID, event ID and a normalized time zone. Use half-open windows so adjacent intervals do not count the same event twice. Temporal retrieval supplies the same boundary discipline for document validity, but event streams have additional lateness and completeness issues.

Join events by stable identity

A trace ID, asset ID or incident ID can join logs from several services. Free-text similarity between two error messages is not sufficient to claim they describe the same incident. Apply tenant and asset filters before joining, then retain each event's source and original timestamp. A repeated warning may be a retry of one operation or many separate failures; deduplicate only with a stable event or request identity. Duplicate evidence rules keep retries from inflating a count.

Treat gaps as unknown

No retrieved alarm is not proof that no alarm occurred. The collector may have been offline, the index may lag, or the query may cover a shard not searched. Record source watermarks and missing intervals. When a window is incomplete, report the covered interval and abstain from a global zero count. A late event can change a previously computed result; either revise the answer or pin it to a snapshot and explain the cutoff. Freshness controls should expose that cutoff in the trace.

Separate retrieval from aggregation

Retrieve the eligible events first, then compute counts, maxima or sequences deterministically. A p95 latency claim requires enough samples and an explicit percentile method; a single high value is not the percentile. For a sequence question, preserve ordering by event time and break ties with stable IDs. Apply units and sampling rates before combining sensor readings. Numeric context is as important for telemetry as it is for a table cell.

Evaluate late and partial data

Build cases with out-of-order arrivals, clock skew, duplicate retries, collector outages, overlapping windows and no matching events. Judge event recall, window-boundary correctness, join identity, completeness detection and final answer support separately. A high recall score on available records can still mask an incorrect 'nothing happened' answer when a source is missing. Keep both query time and data snapshot in the evaluation record so later backfills do not silently change the expected result.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AlarmEvent:
    event_id: str
    tenant: str
    asset_id: str
    occurred_at: datetime
    observed_at: datetime

def window_events(events: list[AlarmEvent], tenant: str, asset_id: str,
                  start: datetime, end: datetime) -> list[str]:
    if start.tzinfo is None or end.tzinfo is None or end <= start:
        raise ValueError("window needs ordered aware datetimes")
    seen: set[str] = set()
    selected: list[str] = []
    for event in sorted(events, key=lambda item: (item.occurred_at, item.event_id)):
        if event.tenant == tenant and event.asset_id == asset_id \
                and start <= event.occurred_at < end and event.event_id not in seen:
            seen.add(event.event_id)
            selected.append(event.event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
event_time = datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 17, tzinfo=utc)
alarms = [AlarmEvent("alarm-47", "north", "P-47", event_time,
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 39, tzinfo=utc)),
          AlarmEvent("alarm-47", "north", "P-47", event_time,
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 40, tzinfo=utc))]
assert window_events(alarms, "north", "P-47",
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 0, tzinfo=utc),
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 30, tzinfo=utc)) == ["alarm-47"]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N events costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space in the example; an index ordered by tenant, asset and event time narrows production windows. Watermarks and coverage records add modest metadata but are necessary for trustworthy zero-result answers. Wider windows increase scanned events and aggregation cost, so apply a query limit and stream large results.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering by collector arrival time when the question asks when an event occurred.
  • Calling an incomplete window empty.
  • Counting duplicate retries as independent alarms.
  • Using naive local timestamps across a daylight-saving boundary.

Validation drill

Build 67 events over three assets with delayed arrivals and two collector gaps. Judge 31 window questions, requiring correct half-open boundaries and an explicit incomplete-data result where coverage is missing.

title: Entity linking for retrieval: resolve aliases before searching facts
summary: Map mentions to stable entity IDs while retaining ambiguity, alias provenance and out-of-catalog behavior.
body:
Map mentions to stable entity IDs while retaining ambiguity, alias provenance and out-of-catalog behavior.

Separate mention from identity

Entity linking maps a surface mention in a query to a canonical entity ID. 'P-47' might identify a pump in one plant and a permit in another; spelling alone is not identity. Store type, tenant, site, active interval and reviewed aliases with each entity. Preserve the original mention in the search trace, and do not replace it with a canonical ID until context establishes the match. Multilingual retrieval may supply transliterated aliases, but an alias can still be shared by distinct entities.

Generate candidates then decide

Exact alias search produces candidates. Type constraints, nearby words, site and time narrow them; semantic similarity can rank the remainder. Keep a no-match outcome for an unknown entity instead of forcing every mention onto the closest catalog entry. If two candidates remain plausible, ask for a clarifier or search both as explicitly separate interpretations. Conversation state can supply an antecedent, but an old assistant answer is not authoritative identity evidence.

Carry identity through evidence

After linking, retrieve passages tagged with the stable entity ID and current authorization scope. A document can mention several entities, so a page-level tag may be too coarse: the cited span must actually refer to the selected entity. If an entity is renamed, maintain alias history and effective dates rather than rewriting old documents. If IDs are merged or split, preserve the mapping event; otherwise historical citations can point to a different object. Chunk identity and entity identity solve different problems and both belong in the trace.

Guard against alias poisoning

User-submitted content may claim that an unrelated part number is an alias for a restricted asset. Accept aliases only from reviewed catalog changes, not from retrieved passages or prompt text. Apply access checks to candidate IDs and to their associated documents; even an ambiguous candidate list can leak a private device name. Normalize Unicode carefully, but do not erase distinctions that matter in identifiers. Tool boundaries keep source text from changing the resolver's catalog.

Evaluate more than top-one accuracy

Judge exact aliases, spelling changes, transliterations, shared names, unknown entities and historical renames. Measure candidate recall, correct-ID selection, abstention for unknown mentions, and downstream supported answers. A top-one metric alone rewards a resolver that confidently guesses on every unknown name. Track entity type and language slices separately. Review cases where linking is correct but the retrieved passage refers to a different entity in the same document; that is an evidence-span error, not a linking success.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CatalogEntity:
    entity_id: str
    tenant: str
    kind: str
    site: str
    aliases: tuple[str, ...]

def alias_key(value: str) -> str:
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", value).casefold().strip()

def resolve_entity(catalog: list[CatalogEntity], tenant: str, kind: str,
                   site: str, mention: str) -> str | None:
    matches = [entry.entity_id for entry in catalog
               if entry.tenant == tenant and entry.kind == kind and entry.site == site
               and alias_key(mention) in {alias_key(alias) for alias in entry.aliases}]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("ambiguous alias; request clarification")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

catalog = [CatalogEntity("pump-47-north", "north", "pump", "plant-a", ("P-47", "Pump 47")),
           CatalogEntity("permit-47-north", "north", "permit", "plant-a", ("P-47",)),
           CatalogEntity("pump-47-south", "south", "pump", "plant-b", ("P-47",))]
assert resolve_entity(catalog, "north", "pump", "plant-a", "P-47") == "pump-47-north"
assert resolve_entity(catalog, "north", "pump", "plant-a", "P-48") is None

Performance and operating cost

The transparent scan checks N catalog entries and up to A aliases per entry, costing O(NA) time with temporary alias sets. An alias index keyed by normalized mention, tenant and type reduces candidate lookup, but it must update atomically with catalog changes. Preserve multiple candidates until context resolves them; forcing one ID can be cheaper per query but costlier in downstream incorrect answers.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a shared alias as a globally unique entity ID.
  • Forcing unknown mentions onto the nearest catalog item.
  • Letting retrieved text edit the trusted alias catalog.
  • Tagging a whole document as support when its cited span refers to another entity.

Validation drill

Create 83 mentions across two tenants and three entity types, including 17 ambiguous aliases and nine unknowns. Score correct IDs, ambiguity handling, unknown abstention and supported downstream passages.

title: Counterfactual retrieval tests: change one fact and trace the failure
summary: Probe retrieval and answer support with controlled evidence edits, plausible distractors and first-loss diagnosis.
body:
Probe retrieval and answer support with controlled evidence edits, plausible distractors and first-loss diagnosis.

Change one controlled variable

A counterfactual retrieval test alters an evidence fact while keeping the rest of the query and corpus stable. Replace a pump limit of 83 kPa with 67 kPa in a synthetic revision, or swap the relevant entity ID, then check whether retrieval and the answer respond to that change. The point is to expose reliance on memorized or distracting text. Use synthetic, clearly isolated fixtures; never mutate a production source or present a test revision as a real policy. Release evaluation can run these cases as a separate judged slice.

Keep labels and access coherent

When a fact changes, update the gold passage, expected answer, revision metadata and all copied evidence that derives from it. Leave unrelated passages unchanged. A distractor can be highly similar yet invalid because its entity, date, tenant or negation differs. If the counterfactual version conflicts with a legitimate original left in the same eligible corpus, the expected behavior may be conflict reporting, not a forced new number. Lineage controls help distinguish an accidental duplicate from independent contradictory evidence.

Locate the first loss

Trace whether the edited passage enters the lexical or vector candidate pool, survives filters and reranking, reaches the context window, and supports the final claim. A wrong answer with the correct passage in context is an answer-use failure; a correct answer after the passage was excluded may indicate memorization or leakage. Do not call both failures 'retrieval quality'. Retrieval traces should carry candidate IDs and score stages so the first bad decision is visible.

Probe distractors without gaming them

Vary one failure mode at a time: wrong part number, old revision, copied note, negated sentence, unit mismatch or unauthorized source. Include a genuinely unanswerable case. A model might pass a simple value swap but fail when the old value appears in a top-ranked stale document. Keep distractor language natural and the target question unchanged. Avoid test cases whose answer is visible in the file name or test label. Hard-negative audits keep distractors from accidentally becoming valid answers.

Report stability and sensitivity

The system should remain stable when irrelevant text changes and change when the supporting fact changes. Measure candidate recall, supported top-one answer, contradiction detection and abstention for each perturbation type. Compare against the same corpus snapshot and model versions. A pass rate that averages easy no-op edits with hard entity swaps obscures the actual weakness; keep per-perturbation slices. Review a sample of failures manually to confirm that the synthetic edit did not create an unintended second answer.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceRecord:
    passage_id: str
    entity_id: str
    revision: str
    value_kpa: int

def answer_limit(records: list[EvidenceRecord], entity_id: str,
                 revision: str) -> int | None:
    matches = [record.value_kpa for record in records
               if record.entity_id == entity_id and record.revision == revision]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("conflicting eligible evidence")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

original = EvidenceRecord("manual-p47-r4", "pump-p47", "r4", 83)
distractor = EvidenceRecord("manual-p48-r4", "pump-p48", "r4", 83)
edited = replace(original, value_kpa=67)
assert answer_limit([original, distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") == 83
assert answer_limit([edited, distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") == 67
assert answer_limit([distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") is None

Performance and operating cost

Creating a synthetic variant costs O(C) for C copied records and running the baseline scan costs O(C) time with O(K) match space. The real expense is repeated retrieval and answer generation across perturbation suites. Keep fixtures small and deterministic for every commit, then run a wider judged sample before a release. Store only synthetic values in test logs so a reviewer cannot confuse them with production facts.

Common Mistakes

  • Changing a value without changing its expected answer and revision label.
  • Leaving an eligible original passage that makes the edited answer ambiguous.
  • Calling a memorized correct answer a retrieval success when evidence never entered context.
  • Averaging all perturbation types into one score that hides a severe slice failure.

Validation drill

Construct 47 synthetic question variants across value, entity, negation, date and permission edits. Record the first pipeline stage that loses the required evidence and whether the final answer changes only when it should.

title: Multimodal retrieval: connect images, OCR and text to one asset identity
summary: Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.
body:
Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.

Define the asset graph

A diagram may have a text caption, OCR labels, a surrounding paragraph and a visual embedding. Give all views one immutable asset revision, then store their own modality and location. A match in OCR is evidence for visible words, not for a visual relation that OCR cannot read. A visual similarity match locates candidate images; it does not prove that two valves have the same operating limit. Source provenance must survive the modality change.

Retrieve and fuse carefully

Text queries can search captions and OCR; image queries can use visual embeddings. Fuse candidate asset IDs only after permission and revision checks. Preserve the match route in the result: caption, OCR, surrounding text or image similarity. This matters when a reviewer asks why a drawing ranked first. Rerank with the full question and a bounded set of candidate assets, not a collection of detached crop embeddings.

Resolve the cited region

An answer about a label in the upper-left crop should cite that region and its parent page. Store normalized crop coordinates and the original image dimensions so a viewer can highlight the right area. If preprocessing rotates or resizes the image, transform coordinates back before presenting them. A citation to an entire manual page may be too broad when the claim depends on a tiny annotation. Support checks should confirm the cited modality can prove the claim.

Measure modality-specific misses

Maintain query slices for exact OCR strings, paraphrased captions, visual resemblance and questions requiring both text and image. Evaluate candidate recall by modality and asset revision. A high combined score can conceal that OCR systematically misses rotated labels. Keep a no-answer slice where a visually similar image lacks the requested label, and require the system to say so.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AssetView:
    asset_id: str
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    modality: str
    content: str

def find_label(views: list[AssetView], label: str, tenant: str,
               active_revisions: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted({view.asset_id for view in views
                   if view.tenant == tenant and view.modality == "ocr"
                   and active_revisions.get(view.asset_id) == view.revision
                   and label.casefold() in view.content.casefold()})

views = [AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r2", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 73 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-b", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa")]
assert find_label(views, "47 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == ["pump-47"]
assert find_label(views, "73 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == []

Performance and operating cost

The sample scans V views in O(V) time and uses O(A) result space for A matching assets. Production retrieval can index each modality, but storage and embedding work grow with the number of views and crops. Set crop limits and deduplicate near-identical renders; otherwise one document can flood the candidate window.

Common Mistakes

  • Using visual similarity as proof of a printed numeric label.
  • Returning a crop without its parent asset and revision.
  • Mixing a fresh caption with OCR from an old image revision.
  • Showing a broad page citation when only one crop supports the answer.

Validation drill

Index 17 diagrams with captions and OCR, including three rotated scans and two superseded revisions. Judge exact-label, visual and mixed queries separately; verify every cited crop opens at the correct page and coordinates.

title: Temporal retrieval: answer as-of questions from valid evidence
summary: Distinguish when a fact was true from when it was indexed, and resolve overlapping revisions before producing a dated answer.
body:
Distinguish when a fact was true from when it was indexed, and resolve overlapping revisions before producing a dated answer.

Store two clocks

Temporal retrieval answers questions about a specified point in time. A policy may be valid from 1 March to 30 June yet ingested on 4 March. Valid time describes when the policy applies; system time describes when the search system learned or changed it. Conflating the two makes historical answers wrong after a late upload or backdated correction. Record both intervals and the source revision. Index freshness explains availability, while valid time determines which fact belongs in the answer.

Parse the user's time boundary

An as-of question needs a date, time zone and boundary convention. 'On 30 June' may mean any instant that day; an interval ending at midnight on 30 June may already be invalid then. Choose half-open intervals consistently: start inclusive, end exclusive. If the user gives only a month, do not quietly pick its last day for a rule that changed mid-month. Ask for a date or return the change range. Query routing should preserve the time constraint across every retrieval leg.

Filter before ranking

Restrict candidates to the requested valid-time interval and authorized corpus before semantic ranking. A newer policy is often lexically similar and may rank above the old one even when the user asks about last year. An answer must cite the applicable revision and the effective interval. For a comparison across dates, retrieve each date separately and keep the two evidence sets distinct. A revision's publication timestamp is not a substitute for its effective timestamp.

Resolve overlap explicitly

Two active records may cover the same instant because of a correction, overlapping jurisdiction or bad source data. Prefer a documented supersession rule only if the source provides one. Otherwise report the conflict with both citations and abstain from a single definitive value. A deletion may remove public availability without erasing the historical audit record; retrieval policy decides whether that archived evidence remains eligible. Access control applies even to historical answers.

Judge temporal slices

Build cases just before and after effective boundaries, retroactive corrections, delayed ingestion, unknown end dates, conflicting overlaps and no eligible history. Measure valid-revision recall and answer support separately from plain passage recall. A search that finds the right policy family but the wrong revision should fail the dated slice. Keep the corpus generation in the judgment so a changing source does not invalidate the comparison.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PolicyRevision:
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    valid_from: date
    valid_until: date | None
    refund_days: int

def applicable_policy(revisions: list[PolicyRevision], tenant: str,
                      as_of: date) -> PolicyRevision | None:
    matches = [policy for policy in revisions if policy.tenant == tenant
               and policy.valid_from <= as_of
               and (policy.valid_until is None or as_of < policy.valid_until)]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("overlapping eligible policy revisions")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

policies = [PolicyRevision("r3", "north", date(2026, 3, 1), date(2026, 7, 1), 47),
            PolicyRevision("r4", "north", date(2026, 7, 1), None, 29),
            PolicyRevision("private", "south", date(2026, 3, 1), None, 83)]
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 6, 30)).refund_days == 47
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 7, 1)).refund_days == 29
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 2, 28)) is None

Performance and operating cost

The example scans R revisions in O(R) time and stores O(M) matches, where M is the number valid at the requested instant. A database interval index and tenant key can reduce candidate reads. Store valid-time and ingestion-time metadata separately; two extra timestamps are cheap compared with an unsupported historical answer.

Common Mistakes

  • Using ingestion time as the policy's effective date.
  • Treating an interval end as inclusive in one service and exclusive in another.
  • Returning the newest revision for every historical question.
  • Silently choosing one of two overlapping eligible revisions.

Validation drill

Create 61 dated questions around four policy transitions, including six backdated corrections and five overlaps. Require explicit ambiguity when the source cannot determine the applicable revision.

title: Multilingual retrieval without losing names, units or permissions
summary: Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.
body:
Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.

Treat language as a retrieval constraint

Multilingual retrieval finds evidence when the question and the answer-bearing document use different languages or scripts. A Hindi request for a pump's pressure limit might need an English maintenance sheet. Translate or encode the request for candidate generation, but retain the original request and its entity spans. A translated product name can become a common noun; a model number or unit can be silently changed. Keep the original tokens beside any expansion so the exact identifier remains searchable. Expansion tests should fail when an alias changes the requested entity.

Use two candidate paths

A multilingual vector index can find semantically related passages across languages; an exact or transliterated term index can recover names and part numbers that an embedding misses. Merge bounded candidate lists, then rank the original passages. Transliteration is a controlled alias for a named entity, not a general translation engine. Store aliases with locale, entity ID and review status. If two entities share the same Roman spelling, an alias must not erase that ambiguity. Hybrid merging gives a practical way to combine the two paths without pretending their raw scores are comparable.

Preserve the source's meaning

Retrieve source text, revision, locale and passage ID together. A translated display excerpt may help the reader, but the citation must still point to the original passage. Numbers, negation, effective dates and units require explicit checks across the translation boundary. Do not answer a question in the user's language from a passage whose translation has inverted 'must not' or converted 47 psi into 47 kPa. Claim-level support is judged against the source, not against a fluent paraphrase.

Filter before mixing languages

Tenant permissions, document status and jurisdiction apply to every language variant. A public English summary is not evidence that a private Spanish appendix can be searched or surfaced. Deduplicate translations by source lineage only after access filtering; separate independently authored statements even if they are translated similarly. Track source revision across language copies because a translated page may lag behind the original. Corpus lifecycle determines which variant is eligible.

Evaluate language pairs, not one average

Build judged queries for each query-language and document-language pair, including mixed-script queries, transliterated names, similar identifiers and documents with no valid answer. Report candidate recall, supported answer rate and entity preservation per pair. A strong English-English score can hide total failure on Hindi-English or Arabic-English searches. Review wrong answers with both original and translated passages. If no reviewer can establish the meaning of the source, mark support unknown rather than accepting the answer by fluency.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ServicePassage:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    locale: str
    text: str
    entity_id: str

def normalized(text: str) -> str:
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).casefold()

def exact_entity_candidates(passages: list[ServicePassage], tenant: str,
                            requested_entity: str, aliases: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    entity_id = aliases.get(normalized(requested_entity))
    if entity_id is None:
        return []
    return [passage.passage_id for passage in passages
            if passage.tenant == tenant and passage.entity_id == entity_id]

service_notes = [ServicePassage("sheet-en-r4", "north", "en",
                                "Pump P-47 relief limit is 83 kPa.", "pump-p47"),
                 ServicePassage("sheet-hi-r2", "south", "hi",
                                "P-47 limit is 99 kPa.", "pump-p47")]
reviewed_aliases = {normalized("पी-47"): "pump-p47", normalized("P-47"): "pump-p47"}
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "पी-47", reviewed_aliases) == ["sheet-en-r4"]
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "P-48", reviewed_aliases) == []

Performance and operating cost

The transparent candidate scan costs O(N) time over N passages and O(K) output space for K eligible matches. A production entity index keyed by tenant and entity ID reduces lookup work but requires reviewed aliases and refreshes when documents change. A second multilingual vector path adds index storage and query latency; measure its incremental supported recall by language pair before accepting the cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating transliteration as an unambiguous entity identifier.
  • Dropping the original query after translation and losing exact numbers or negation.
  • Citing only a generated translation rather than the source passage.
  • Reporting one aggregate recall score across uneven language pairs.

Validation drill

Build 53 questions across three query languages and two document languages. Include twelve mixed-script identifiers and eight restricted passages. Record entity preservation, authorized candidate recall and supported answers for every language pair.

title: Retrieval release gates: evaluate slices before changing an index
summary: Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.
body:
Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.

Freeze the comparison

Store query, permitted corpus snapshot, expected answer-bearing passage IDs, acceptable abstention and query family. Run current and candidate versions against the same access snapshot. Keep exact IDs, paraphrases, multilingual queries, long documents, stale revisions and no-answer cases separate. A global average can rise while one small tenant loses its only correct passage. Retrieval and answer quality remain separate measurements.

Measure decisions

For each query, measure answer-bearing candidate recall, required-fact survival in the final packet, first relevant rank and unsupported answer claims. Record p95 latency and forbidden-passage exposure; the latter must stay at zero. Some questions have no answer, so abstention matters. Compare equal cutoffs and token budgets across versions.

Set slice floors before testing

Write thresholds before seeing candidate results. A release may require no access violations, no decline in exact-ID recall and a bounded p95 increase while accepting a defined paraphrase improvement. Such thresholds are product policies, not universal constants. Inspect every newly failed query and retain it for regression work.

Canary and recover

After offline gates pass, send a small permitted traffic slice to the candidate alias and watch latency, empty-result rate and citation resolution before widening. Record encoder, extraction, corpus, filter and ranker revisions. Rollback query encoder and index alias together. Embedding migrations fail quietly when only one half is reverted.

Worked contract

def release_decision(current: dict, candidate: dict) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    failures = []
    if candidate["access_violations"] != 0:
        failures.append("access violation")
    if candidate["exact_id_recall"] < current["exact_id_recall"]:
        failures.append("exact-ID recall regression")
    if candidate["answer_support"] < current["answer_support"]:
        failures.append("answer support regression")
    if candidate["p95_ms"] > current["p95_ms"] + 47:
        failures.append("latency budget exceeded")
    return not failures, failures

baseline = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .94,
            "answer_support": .91, "p95_ms": 168}
candidate = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .95,
             "answer_support": .92, "p95_ms": 199}
assert release_decision(baseline, candidate) == (True, [])
assert release_decision(baseline, {**candidate, "access_violations": 1})[0] is False

Performance and operating cost

Evaluation of Q queries and K candidates costs at least O(QK) identity work, plus search, rerank and answer calls. Keep a small smoke set for each change and a broader judged set before promotion. The 47 ms allowance in this example is product-specific; choose a measured budget for the actual service.

Common Mistakes

  • Promoting on one average while an important tenant slice regresses.
  • Changing the judged corpus between baseline and candidate runs.
  • Reporting answer quality without candidate recall or access exposure.
  • Rolling back the index while leaving the new query encoder active.

Validation drill

Build 120 judged questions across six slices. Compare two generations at identical top-12 and 600-token packet limits, list newly failed queries and record the rollback target.
